objectives: Reason about energy markets + transition pathways.

slides.title: LCOE: levelized cost of energy
slides.body:
**LCOE** = total lifetime cost / total lifetime energy generated. The standard metric for comparing generation technologies.
$$\text{LCOE} = \frac{\sum_t \frac{C_t + O_t + F_t}{(1+r)^t}}{\sum_t \frac{E_t}{(1+r)^t}}$$
Where $C_t$ = capex, $O_t$ = opex, $F_t$ = fuel cost, $E_t$ = energy, $r$ = discount rate.

**Discount rate $r$** captures cost of capital + opportunity cost. Higher $r$ = penalizes long-lived high-capex projects. Major sensitivity for nuclear, hydro (long life); less for gas peakers (short payback).

**LCOE 2024 estimates (USA, no subsidies)**:
- Utility solar: \$25-50/MWh.
- Onshore wind: \$30-60/MWh.
- Offshore wind: \$60-90/MWh.
- Battery storage (4 hr): \$80-150/MWh ($/MWh of services delivered).
- Natural gas (CCGT): \$45-75/MWh + carbon costs.
- Coal: \$60-100/MWh + carbon costs.
- Nuclear (existing): \$30-60/MWh.
- Nuclear (new): \$80-130/MWh.
- Geothermal: \$50-80/MWh.
- Hydro: \$25-50/MWh.

**Important caveats**:
- LCOE compares LIKE TO LIKE — variable wind + solar are NOT directly comparable to dispatchable gas/nuclear at high renewable penetration.
- LCOE excludes integration costs (transmission, storage, balancing). 'System LCOE' accounts for these.
- Subsidies + tax credits make sticker prices misleading. IRA's solar PTC + battery ITC effectively halve solar+storage costs in USA 2024+.

**Capacity factor** assumed in LCOE: solar ~25%, wind 35%, gas 50-80%, nuclear 92%.

**Modern variable-renewable LCOE includes 'firming' costs**: storage, transmission, balancing. Adds typically \$20-40/MWh.

**Trends**:
- Solar PV: ~10%/year cost decline since 2010.
- Wind onshore: ~3-5%/year.
- Battery storage: ~10-15%/year decline.
- Gas: stable; carbon pricing + supply variability dominate.
- Nuclear new builds: cost escalations (Vogtle USA, Hinkley UK).

**Why solar + wind have won on cost**:
- Manufacturing scale + learning curves (Wright's law: each doubling of cumulative production → ~20% cost decline).
- Modular: can build small or large; iterative improvements.
- No fuel cost variability.
- Fast permitting + construction (vs nuclear's 5-10 years).

slides.title: Carbon pricing + market mechanisms
slides.body:
**Carbon price**: monetary value of CO₂ emissions. Internalizes the externality.

**Why it matters**: without pricing carbon, emitters get an effective subsidy (society bears cost). With pricing, market reflects true cost.

**Implementation mechanisms**:

**Carbon tax**: fixed price per ton of CO₂. Simple. UK, Sweden (\$120/t — highest), Singapore, Canada (\$65/t rising to \$170 by 2030).

**Cap-and-trade (Emissions Trading System, ETS)**: government issues finite emission allowances; companies trade them. Price emerges from market.
- **EU ETS**: largest. ~\$60-90/t (2023-2024). Covers ~40% of EU emissions.
- **California Cap-and-Trade**: ~\$30-40/t.
- **RGGI** (Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, NE USA): ~\$15/t.
- **China ETS**: launched 2021, currently \$10-15/t.
- **UK ETS**: similar to EU after Brexit.

**Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)**: tariff on imports based on embedded carbon. EU implementing 2026+. Prevents 'leakage' (factories moving to avoid carbon costs).

**Free permits + revenues**: allowance allocation matters. EU: ~50% auctioned, rest free (declining). Revenue funds climate programs.

**Effective carbon prices required for Paris Agreement**:
- High Ambition: \$50-100/t by 2030, \$100-200/t by 2050.
- Current global average: ~\$5-10/t.
- Major gap.

**Subsidies for renewables**:
- **Investment Tax Credit (ITC)**: percent of capex. USA: 30% for solar + storage.
- **Production Tax Credit (PTC)**: per-MWh of energy. USA: \$26/MWh for wind.
- **Feed-in tariffs**: guaranteed price for renewable generation (Germany, Spain pioneered, declining as renewables become cost-competitive).
- **CfD (Contracts for Difference)**: UK + EU. Guarantee strike price; market difference paid by/to consumers. Used for offshore wind, nuclear.

**IRA (Inflation Reduction Act, USA 2022)**: \$370B for clean energy + electric vehicles. Largest USA climate investment. ITC, PTC, hydrogen credits, manufacturing incentives. Has unleashed unprecedented US clean-energy investment.

**Subsidies in other regions**: EU Green Deal, Japan GX, China subsidies (now phasing out as costs fall), India PM-KUSUM, Brazil REIDI.

slides.title: Energy markets + the transition challenge
slides.body:
**Wholesale electricity markets**:
- **Energy market**: buy/sell power for delivery in specific hours. Day-ahead + real-time. Marginal pricing — last unit dispatched sets price for all.
- **Capacity market**: pays generators just for being available (regardless of energy delivery). Some markets (PJM, ISO-NE).
- **Ancillary services**: frequency response, voltage support, reserves.
- **Renewable shifting**: solar-heavy regions see negative prices during day (oversupply); high prices at sunset.

**LCOE vs LACE**: LCOE is supply cost; LACE (Levelized Avoided Cost of Energy) reflects market value. Solar's market value DROPS at high penetration as midday glut depresses prices.

**Capacity factor + value factor**: high renewable penetration → declining value factor (each new MWh worth less). Drives need for storage + transmission.

**Transition costs**:
- IEA 2050 Net-Zero: \$200T cumulative investment (2020s-2050s) globally. Most in clean generation + transmission + buildings + transport.
- Trillions per year. Roughly comparable to today's global energy investment but redirected.
- Returns: avoided climate damages, reduced air pollution, energy security.

**Stranded assets**: existing fossil-fuel infrastructure becoming uneconomic as transition accelerates. Estimated \$1-4 trillion of fossil assets globally. Asset owners + creditors at risk. Drives political resistance.

**Just transition**: ensure workers + communities affected by fossil-fuel decline have alternatives. Coal-region rebuilding (Appalachia, Ruhr Valley). Worker retraining. Pension protections. Climate justice considerations.

**The transition timeline**:
- IPCC 1.5°C: peak emissions by 2025, 43% reduction by 2030, net-zero by 2050.
- Current Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs): ~2.5-2.8°C trajectory.
- Gap: ~50% additional reduction needed beyond NDC.
- Investment in clean energy growing rapidly (~\$2T/year in 2024) but needs to ~triple.

**Politics + the energy transition**:
- Strong renewable cost economics now make many policies easier.
- Political fights over: subsidy levels, transmission siting, nuclear's role, gas as 'bridge fuel', timing of fossil-fuel phase-out.
- Climate movement + voter pressure increasingly important.
- Geopolitics: renewables shift power dynamics (less dependence on oil-exporting nations; new dependence on minerals, manufacturing).

**Outlook**: energy transition is real, accelerating, + roughly on cost-trajectory. The pace + politics + equity dimensions remain the questions, not the underlying physics or economics.

question.question: Compute LCOE for solar + battery
question.goal: Solar PV: \$1/W capex, 25% CF, 25-yr life, 7% discount, \$15/kW-yr fixed O&M. Battery: \$1500/kW (4-hr), 90% RTE, 15-yr life. Compute LCOE for solar alone.

steps.prompt: Annual energy from 1 kW solar at 25% CF: $1 \times 8760 \times 0.25 = ?$
CRF (Capital Recovery Factor) for 7%, 25 yr: $CRF = r/(1-(1+r)^{-n}) \approx 0.086$. Annualized capex: \$1000 × 0.086 = ?
Total annual cost per kW: \$86 + \$15 = \$101/kW-yr. LCOE = \$101 / 2190 = ?

Add 4-hr battery storage: \$1500/kW capex. Brings firmness but adds cost. Without going through full math, expect LCOE increase to ~\$70-100/MWh for solar+storage 'firm'. The key is: solar+storage is now cheaper than gas + carbon. What does this trajectory mean?

options: Solar + storage approaching firm-gas cost without carbon adder; with carbon pricing or IRA subsidies, solar+storage ALREADY cheaper than gas in many markets. This is THE economic foundation of the energy transition.

steps.reveal: Solar+storage at firm equivalent cost is now competitive (often cheaper) than gas-with-carbon. With subsidies, MUCH cheaper. This is why solar+storage deployment is accelerating exponentially. The economic transition is real + accelerating.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{LCOE} = \frac{\text{Annualized capex + O\&M + fuel}}{\text{Annual energy}}}$$ LCOE is the workhorse comparison metric. For variable resources (solar + wind), 'firm LCOE' or 'value-adjusted LCOE' is more meaningful when grid penetration is high. The continued cost decline of solar + wind + storage + grid integration is the engine of the energy transition. Models + scenarios + investments all hinge on these numbers.

question.question: Why is carbon pricing widely considered the most economically efficient climate policy?
options: Carbon price internalizes externality — emitters face true cost of CO₂. Market allocates reductions to cheapest options. Single price gives every actor (producers, consumers, investors) the same signal. Other policies (mandates, subsidies) are more distortionary or expensive.
question.explanation: Economist consensus: carbon pricing is the most efficient tool because it (1) internalizes externality at lowest deadweight loss; (2) lets market find cheapest abatement; (3) gives long-term price signal for investment; (4) is technology-neutral. EU ETS, UK ETS, California carbon market all work in practice. Political reality: carbon pricing politically harder than subsidies (visible cost). Most countries use a MIX: some carbon price + subsidies + standards. The IEA + IMF + IPCC all recommend higher carbon prices. Current global average ~\$5-10/t; need ~\$100/t by 2050 for Paris.

slides.workedSolution: Efficiency: single price signal, market finds cheapest cuts, technology-neutral, gives investment signal. Why not everywhere: political resistance (visible cost), distributional concerns (regressive without rebates), lobbying. Best practice: combine with rebates (Canada returns most revenue to households) + targeted subsidies. The economist consensus is firm; the political execution varies.

question.question: Renewable investment thesis
question.prompt: An investor evaluates a 500 MW solar project with battery storage. Walk through the LCOE + IRR + risk analysis.
Explain in two or three sentences why the energy transition is increasingly DRIVEN BY ECONOMICS rather than just policy.
question.rubric: Mentions that solar + wind + storage have become cheapest new generation in most markets without subsidies (LCOE crossing fossil thresholds); private investment is flooding in (~\$2T/year + growing); policy + subsidies amplify but underlying economic competitiveness is real. The transition is now self-sustaining + accelerating; the remaining questions are pace + equity + grid integration rather than 'can we afford it'.
